name: Berlin Defense
summary: The Berlin Defense (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6) is a rock-solid Ruy Lopez counterattack famed for its drawish Berlin Wall endgame.
intro: The Berlin Defense arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6, an old and stubbornly reliable answer to the Ruy Lopez in which Black immediately counterattacks the e4-pawn instead of the customary Morphy move 3...a6. Rather than fighting for space, Black aims for structural soundness and long-term resilience, steering the game toward the technical positions in which the defense excels. Its reputation rests on the celebrated Berlin Wall endgame, a fortress-like structure that has frustrated attackers at every level. Endgame-oriented and defensively resourceful, it is one of the most respected drawing weapons in modern chess.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining idea of the Berlin is the trade of activity for structure. By meeting 3.Bb5 with 3...Nf6, Black challenges e4 at once, and in the main line 4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the queens leave the board very early. Black voluntarily surrenders the right to castle and accepts doubled c-pawns, but receives the bishop pair and a remarkably solid, low-risk position with no obvious weaknesses to attack.

Play then revolves around a subtle endgame struggle. White tries to exploit the extra kingside pawn majority and Black's displaced king, often gaining space and probing on the queenside where Black's structure is doubled. Black, in turn, leans on the two bishops, activates the king toward the center, and neutralizes White's initiative through precise piece placement. The resulting positions are notoriously drawish, rewarding deep technical understanding rather than sharp tactical calculation.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The principal battleground is the open, or Berlin Wall, variation beginning 4.O-O Nxe4. After 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the famous endgame appears, and much of the theory concerns how White develops with moves like Nc3, Rd1+, and h3 to restrict Black's light-squared bishop, while Black coordinates the bishops and reroutes the king to safety. Precise move orders matter greatly here, since a single inaccuracy can hand one side lasting pressure.

Many players who dislike the endgame sidestep it with the Anti-Berlin 4.d3, quietly supporting e4 and keeping queens on the board for a slower, maneuvering middlegame. Other independent tries include 4.O-O Nxe4 5.Re1 and various early deviations, but 4.d3 has become the fashionable way to pose different problems without entering the drawn-out technical waters of the Berlin Wall.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: Though the Berlin Defense is one of the oldest lines in the Ruy Lopez, it spent much of the twentieth century in the shadow of the main-line Morphy Defense. Its modern renaissance came at the very top: Vladimir Kramnik deployed the Berlin Wall to blunt Garry Kasparov's formidable 1.e4 in their 2000 World Championship match, neutralizing the champion's initiative and helping decide the title. That success triggered an enormous revival, and the Berlin has since become a mainstay of elite practice and a benchmark for defensive technique.

keyIdeas: Answer 3.Bb5 by counterattacking e4 with 3...Nf6, not 3...a6.
The main line reaches the drawish Berlin Wall endgame after 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8.
Black trades castling rights and gets doubled c-pawns for the bishop pair.
Queens come off early, favoring technique over tactics.
White can avoid the endgame entirely with the Anti-Berlin 4.d3.
Kramnik's 2000 use against Kasparov sparked its elite revival.

white: Press the kingside pawn majority to create a passed pawn in the endgame.
Restrict Black's light-squared bishop with moves like h3 and Nc3.
Use Rd1+ and rapid development to exploit Black's displaced king.
Choose the Anti-Berlin 4.d3 to keep queens on for a slow middlegame.
Target the queenside where Black's doubled c-pawns are structurally fixed.
black: Activate the bishop pair to control key diagonals and squares.
Reroute the king to safety, often toward c7 or e7, then centralize it.
Blunt White's initiative with precise, solid piece coordination.
Aim for simplification, leaning on the endgame's inherent drawishness.
Meet the Anti-Berlin 4.d3 with sound development and central control.
